facts.statement: Maiaspondylus is an extinct genus of ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaurs found in Canada, England, and Russia.
facts.quote: Maiaspondylus is an extinct genus of platypterygiine ophthalmosaurid ichthyosaurs known from Northwest Territories of Canada, the Cambridge Greensand of England and the Voronezh Region of Russia.

facts.statement: The genus is known from a nearly complete, disarticulated holotype skeleton preserved in three dimensions.
facts.quote: Maiaspondylus is known from the holotype UALVP 45635, a disarticulated but nearly complete skeleton preserved in three dimensions

facts.statement: Referred materials include two articulated embryos found within the body cavity of an adult skeleton.
facts.quote: from the referred materials UALVP 45639, two articulated, partially preserved embryos and eight articulated vertebrae of an adult

facts.statement: All specimens were collected at Hay River from the Loon River Formation, dating to about 110 million years ago.
facts.quote: All specimens were collected at Hay River from the Loon River Formation, dating to the early Albian age of the Early Cretaceous, about 110 million years ago.

facts.statement: The genus was named by Maxwell and Caldwell in 2006, with the type species being Maiaspondylus lindoei.
facts.quote: Maiaspondylus was named by Erin E. Maxwell and Michael W. Caldwell in 2006 and the type species is Maiaspondylus lindoei.

facts.statement: The generic name combines Greek words for "caring mother" and "vertebra".
facts.quote: The generic name is derived from maia (μαία), Greek for "caring mother" and spondylos (σπόνδυλος), Greek for "vertebra".

facts.statement: The specific name honors technician Allan Lindoe for discovering and preparing the specimens.
facts.quote: The specific name honors the Geology Museum of the University of Alberta technician Allan Lindoe for discovering, collecting and preparating the specimens.

facts.statement: Researchers suggested that the presence of embryos inside an adult proves Maiaspondylus was viviparous, giving live birth.
facts.quote: Maxwell and Caldwell (2003) suggested that this specimen proves that Maiaspondylus was viviparous, giving live birth.

facts.statement: The embryos found in Maiaspondylus are the geologically youngest and physically smallest known ichthyosaur embryos.
facts.quote: These embryos are the geologically youngest and the physically smallest known ichthyosaur embryos.

facts.statement: Druckenmiller and Maxwell (2010) found Maiaspondylus most closely related to a species of Platypterygius that likely does not belong to that genus.
facts.quote: Patrick S. Druckenmiller and Erin E. Maxwell (2010) found it to be most closely related to "Platypterygius" americanus, which probably do not belong to the genus Platypterygius.

facts.statement: Specimens were originally referred to Platypterygius, but recent cladistic analyses confirm Maiaspondylus is a valid ophthalmosaurid genus.
facts.quote: Todos los ejemplares de Maiaspondylus fueron originalmente referidos a Platypterygius. Sin embargo, todos los análisis cladísticos recientes han encontrado que Maiaspondylus es un género válido de oftalmosáurido

facts.statement: The holotype is distinguished from other ichthyosaurs by extensive overlapping contact between the jugal and maxilla bones.
facts.quote: dado que el holotipo se distingue de otros ictiosaurios por un amplio contacto superpuesto de los huesos yugal y maxilar

facts.statement: The teeth have smooth crowns, striated cement, lingual curvature, and implantation in a dental groove.
facts.quote: dientes marginales con coronas lisas, con cemento estriado, la curvatura lingual y la implantación en el surco dental

facts.statement: The humerus has isomorphic proximal and distal ends with three distal articular facets, where the medial facet is smaller than the lateral ones.
facts.quote: y el húmero con los extremos proximal y distal isomorfos, con tres facetas articulares distales en que la carilla articular medial es más pequeña que las facetas laterales.

facts.statement: Maiaspondylus lived during the Albian stage of the Early Cretaceous, between 110.1 and 106.3 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Albian to Albian (110.1 to 106.3 million years ago)
